Notes: Year Established basis: earliest documented Jewish presence = founding of Tiberias by Herod Antipas c. 20 CE (Stein dates foundation 17/18-20/21 CE; Miller & Snyder 19/20 CE); the Rakkath identification is tradition only. Josephus, Antiquities 18.36-38 (Whiston): Herod (Antipas) built Tiberias at the lake of Gennesareth; 'Strangers came and inhabited this city; a great number of the inhabitants were Galileans also'; many were compelled by Herod to settle, including persons of condition, poor people and not-quite-freemen given houses and land; the site required removal of many sepulchres, which made settlement a transgression of Jewish law (7-day impurity). Founding event; mixed settler body with many Galilean (Jewish) settlers; no figure.

Founding event: Tiberias 'was founded in 19/20 c.e. by King Herod Antipas as his new capital in Galilee' (Miller & Snyder 2026, BASOR 395, abstract); reassessment of the palace of Antipas excavated by Y. Hirschfeld (original palatial complex, later reused as dwellings probably in 2nd c. CE). Capital of a Jewish tetrarch; no population figure.

c. 20 CE (beginning of 1st c. CE). Theater excavated by Y. Hirschfeld and Y. Stefanski re-dated 'all the way back to the beginning of the 1st century CE' (Haaretz 2009, quoted on BiblePlaces Blog); Hirschfeld: 'Unlike Tzipori, which was a multi-cultural city, Tiberias was a Jewish city under Roman rule' and the theater's interest is 'its Jewish context'. Scholar's characterization of the early city as Jewish; theater capacity (c. 7,000 seats per other pages) is not a population figure.

c. 30 CE (Stein dates it 30/31-31/32 CE). Josephus, Antiquities 18.149: Herod (Antipas) and Herodias 'allotted him [Agrippa, later Agrippa I] Tiberias for his habitation', gave him an income and 'made him a magistrate of that city'. Named Jewish resident (Herodian prince) living in Tiberias; no figure.

Lead market weight of Tiberias dated year 34 of Herod Antipas = 30/31 CE, naming the agoranomos Gaius Julius; A. Stein (ZPE 93, 1992, 144-148) proposes he is the future Jewish king Agrippa I, whom Antipas appointed agoranomos of Tiberias c. 30-32 CE; Stein calls Tiberias 'a small provincial city'. Dated inscription; presence of a (probably Jewish) city official; no figure.

Event: after Antipas was deposed in 39 CE the city was annexed with the rest of his realm to the kingdom of his nephew Agrippa I; after Agrippa's death in 44 it passed to direct Roman rule; coins of 54 CE show the name Claudiopolis (Hebrew Wikipedia). The same page says Antipas settled the city with gentiles, poor and freed slaves and forced Jews to move there. Change of ruler; no figure.

1st c. CE midpoint (c.). Chancey (Bible Interpretation, 2003): Antipas built Tiberias c. 20 CE; archaeological evidence very limited because the ancient city lies under the modern one; 'fragments of stone vessels and of ossuaries used for Jewish secondary burial may be from the first century' (possibly 2nd c.); first-century Antipas coins of Tiberias do not depict deities; a market weight of c. 31 CE names agoranomos Gaius Julius. Presence evidence of Jewish residents (purity vessels, ossuaries), scale not given.

1st-2nd c. CE (midpoint of 1st c. used, c.). NEAEHL entry 'Tiberias' (Stepansky, Hirschfeld, Gutfeld), Galei Kinneret Hotel excavation (M. Hartal 2002): 'Stone "measuring cups" found in this area constitute evidence for the existence of a Jewish community in Tiberias' in the 1st-2nd c. CE, in an area on the lakeshore probably the stadium mentioned by Josephus; the earliest settlement stratum at Tiberias is Early Roman. Archaeological evidence of an organized Jewish community; no figure.

1st c. CE (midpoint used). Wikipedia: 'The city is estimated to have had a population between 4,500 and 15,000 during the first century CE' (citing J. L. Reed, Archaeology and the Galilean Jesus, 2002, p. 82; original not checked). TOTAL population of the city, not Jews only; the same page says Antipas settled many non-Jews there and observant Jews refused to settle, so Population left blank (city mixed per this source; Jewish share not given). Same page: council of 600 with a committee of ten until 44 CE.

1st c. CE / time of Jesus (midpoint used, c.). Fiensy & Strange, Introduction to Galilee vols. 1-2 (Fortress), n. 10: 'Meyers suggests 18,000 for Sepphoris and 24,000 for Tiberias' (E. M. Meyers, 'Jesus and His Galilean Context', 1997, p. 59); compare Reed, Archaeology and the Galilean Jesus, 117. TOTAL population estimate of the city (Jewish share not stated in this source; Tiberias had a Greek minority), so Population left blank.

1st c. CE (midpoint used, c.). Same footnote (Fiensy & Strange, n. 10): 'J. Andrew Overman offered 30,000 to 40,000 for Tiberias' (Overman, SBL 1988 Seminar Papers, 160-68); 'Horsley maintained that both cities together [Sepphoris and Tiberias] had a population of 15,000' (Horsley 1996, p. 45). TOTAL-population estimates (one a two-city aggregate) without a Jewish share in this source; Population left blank. The modern range of estimates spans c. 4,500-40,000.

c. 54/55 CE (passage follows Nero's accession; some modern works date the transfer to 61 CE). Josephus, Antiquities 20.159: 'Caesar also bestowed on Agrippa a certain part of Galilee, Tiberias, and Tarichae' - Tiberias transferred to the Jewish king Agrippa II, losing its status as capital (cf. Life 38). Event; no figure.

Josephus, Life 32-38 (Whiston): at the outbreak of the revolt (66 CE) 'There were three factions in this city': men of worth headed by Julius Capellus with Herod son of Miarus and Herod son of Gamalus (pro-Roman/pro-Agrippa), and a faction headed by Justus son of Pistus, who argued Tiberias had held 'the principal place' under Herod the tetrarch before Nero gave it to Agrippa II. Named Jewish residents and an organized civic community; no figure.

Josephus, Life 64-69 (66 CE): Josephus summoned 'the senate of Tiberias' and its principal men (incl. Justus) and asked them to demolish Antipas's palace 'which had the figures of living creatures in it'; Jesus son of Sapphias, 'leader of a seditious tumult of mariners and poor people', set the palace on fire, and 'Jesus and his party slew all the Greeks that were inhabitants of Tiberias'. Events in the Jewish community; the Greeks killed were the city's non-Jewish residents (number not given).

c. 66/67 CE. Josephus, Life 276-280: the people of Tiberias assembled in the Proseucha (prayer house), 'a large edifice, and capable of receiving a great number of people', with the council; the meeting was broken off at the Sabbath dinner hour. Synagogue building and Sabbath-observing Jewish community; no figure.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (2nd ed., Avi-Yonah et al.) 'Tiberias' on encyclopedia.com: city built between 14 and 18 CE; 'The original population was mixed (Jos., Ant., 18:36ff.), including landless people and freed slaves'; shunned by observant Jews because of tombs; organized on the Greek model with a boule headed by an archon; 'At the time of the First Jewish War, Jewish fishermen comprised the majority of the population'; in 66 split between Zealots and the wealthy pro-Roman party. Jewish majority stated; no figure.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) 'Tiberias': 'The majority of the inhabitants, nevertheless, were Jews'; council (boule) of 500 [sic; Josephus War 2.641 gives 600] with an archon; buildings incl. a proseuche (synagogue), palace and stadium; in 66 three parties (pro-Roman, the mass of the poor supporting the revolt, neutrals incl. Justus of Tiberias); rebels led by archon Jesus ben Zappha. JE dates the founding to 26 CE. Jewish majority stated; no figure.

Weiss 2022, 'Between Two Cities' (Et-Mol 280), abstract: in both Tiberias and Sepphoris 'lived a large and autonomous Jewish population'; per Josephus the Jewish population of both places sided with the Romans against the rebels in the Great Revolt; Tiberias initially more splendid than Sepphoris as Antipas's capital. Qualitative ('large') Jewish population; no figure.

c. winter 66/67 CE. Josephus, War 2.632-646: 'Tiberias revolted again, the people within it inviting king Agrippa'; Josephus seized ten 'of the most potent men of Tiberias', then 'all their senate, consisting of six hundred persons, and about two thousand of the populace' and shipped them to Taricheae as prisoners. 600 = council members and 2,000 = detained subset of the populace (subset/prisoner counts, not total population); Population blank.

67 CE. Josephus, War 3.445-461: Vespasian camped 30 furlongs from Tiberias; the rebel band under 'Jesus, the son of Shaphat' [Sapphias] fled; the elders and principal citizens supplicated Vespasian, 'the citizens opened to him their gates', the south wall was broken down for entry, and Vespasian forbade plunder to gratify King Agrippa II. City surrendered and was spared; Jewish population continued (no destruction, no figure).

67 CE. Josephus, War 3.532-542: after the fall of Taricheae, captives were gathered in the stadium at Tiberias; Vespasian had 1,200 old and useless men killed, sent 6,000 young men to Nero (Isthmus canal) and sold 30,400 as slaves; the captives were Tarichaeans' foreign allies and refugees (Trachonites, Gaulanites, men of Hippos and Gadara), not residents of Tiberias. Casualty/captive counts only; Population blank.
